description: We are a multidisciplinary team passionate about technology, data, AI, Earth science, and creative problem-solving. Our team combines skills in programming, data analysis, AI, research, data visualization, game development, and creative thinking. We aim to explore Earth system trends, understand their impacts, and build innovative, interactive solutions that help people better understand our planet and its future.
summary: What if understanding Earth's changing environment could be both a scientific investigation and an adventure? Introducing **Earth Trend Detective**, an interactive platform that transforms NASA Earth science data into an engaging discovery experience. Our project combines a scientific web application with an adventure-style game. Through the web application, users can explore environmental variables, investigate different locations, and visualize long-term changes through interactive maps and time-series graphs. Going beyond visualization, the platform analyzes trends to reveal their direction, rate of change, and statistical significance using scientific methods such as Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope. But discovering environmental changes is only part of the journey. Our interactive game turns these scientific concepts into an adventure where players explore environmental challenges, examine evidence, and make decisions to protect themselves and their communities. By combining real Earth science analysis with interactive learning, Earth Trend Detective makes complex environmental data more accessible and helps people better understand the changes shaping our planet.
details:
Earth Trend Detective's Project Solution

Earth Trend Detective guides users through one connected journey: discover, verify, connect and act. Place, variable, year and charts stay synchronised in every section, so the investigation never resets.



1.Explore Earth:
Users choose a place by searching, clicking the 3D globe or pressing "Use my location." They then select one of nine Earth-system variables:

  • Air temperature (2 m), from MERRA-2, 1980–2025
  • Land surface (skin) temperature, from GLDAS Noah v2.1, 2000–2025
  • Precipitation, from GPM IMERG Final v07, 1998–2024
  • Root-zone soil moisture, from GLDAS Noah v2.1, 2000–2025
  • Evapotranspiration, from GLDAS Noah v2.1, 2000–2025
  • Surface runoff, from GLDAS Noah v2.1, 2000–2025
  • Snow water equivalent, from GLDAS Noah v2.1, 2000–2025
  • Relative humidity, from AIRS/Aqua v7.0, 2003–2025
  • Tropospheric nitrogen dioxide, from OMI/Aura, 2005–2025

Whole-Earth yearly maps from NASA Giovanni (GPM precipitation, OMI NO2, AIRS humidity and MODIS aerosols) colour the globe. A time slider and clickable climate stripes, one stripe per year, show how the selected variable has evolved. Every time range automatically matches the years for which that variable has data.


2.Before & After:
Before & After compares a place with itself: same boundaries, two different years. The user picks the two years and sees the measured change between them for the selected variable. At featured places, the comparison adds NASA MODIS imagery from AppEEARS of the same area: vegetation (NDVI) images for every July from 2001 to 2025, and true-colour satellite photographs. A satellite time-lapse then plays the change year by year, so users can watch the landscape shift from orbit.



3.Trend Explorer:
Trend Explorer tests every available variable for the selected place automatically and ranks the most significant changes first, whether they are rising or falling. Statistically significant trends lead the list, ordered by signal-to-noise ratio, so users see at once which factors matter most. Each insight card shows a direction arrow, the rate of change, a significance badge and a sparkline.

For each variable, users can open the full time series and see:

  • whether the trend is increasing or decreasing, and how fast, with a 95% confidence interval
  • whether it is statistically significant, with the p-value explained in plain language
  • the emergence year, when the signal rose above natural variability
  • yearly and monthly results side by side, with a note on whether they agree
  • a backtested projection of where the trend is heading, shown only when it beats a no-change forecast

A Place Fingerprint summarises all variables in one radial chart and can be downloaded as an image. A ranking compares the place's warming rate with the planet as a whole, and an optional Lifetime Lens restates every trend as "since you were born.


4.Earth Connections:
Users choose two or three variables and view them on one chart as standardised anomalies. Correlations are calculated after removing each series' trend, so a shared warming signal cannot create a false link. Each pair is labelled either as a known physical mechanism (for example, dry soil heats up because less water evaporates to cool it) or as a pattern only. Users learn that correlation is not causation.

5.Solutions Lab:
The Solutions Lab classifies each place by area type: hot or cold desert, dryland, tropics, temperate, polar, city or countryside, coast and snow. It rates upcoming hazards as Low, Medium or High from the measured trends and backtested projections. These hazards include rising heat, drying land, heavier rain, flood runoff, humid heat, rising water demand, shrinking snowpack and rising NO2.

It then recommends prevention options suited to that area. For each one, it explains:

  • how to apply it in that kind of place
  • its limits, time frame and cost
  • what it changes: temperature, water demand, flood runoff or green cover

Options are organised in a roadmap: now, the next 2–5 years and the long term. Options are filtered by area, so permafrost foundations appear only in polar places and mangroves only on tropical coasts. In Cairo, for example, "Rising heat" leads to cool roofs and pavements, heat early-warning systems with cooling centres, and heat-ready buildings.



6.Glossary
Science in Plain Words
Every scientific term is explained where it appears. An info icon is added automatically next to terms such as Sen's slope, Mann-Kendall, p-value, anomaly and evapotranspiration. Tapping it opens a short card with the plain meaning, the scientific definition and a real example from the selected place, such as Cairo's measured mean skin temperature. The full glossary holds 45 terms and is searchable from the header at any time.

7. Tools for Every User

  • Tutorial: a step-by-step walkthrough on the first visit, replayable at any time.
  • Guided Story: a narrated tour of a place, from "what is changing" to "what can be done."
  • Dashboard: opened from the header button, it shows every variable for one place on a single screen: headline figures, a tile per variable with its chart and projection, and a table of all statistics. A "Download summary report" button is built in.
  • Summary Report: a self-contained report of findings, projections, charts, statistics and sources, ready to print or save as PDF.
  • Shareable links: each view can be shared as a link that reopens it exactly.

Downloads: users can take their findings with them in three formats. The Place Fingerprint downloads as a PNG image from the Trend Explorer. The Summary Report downloads as an HTML file, which can be printed or saved as PDF, from the Dashboard or the Explore panel. The raw data for any variable downloads as a CSV file from the Explore panel.

The Protector: You (the adventure game):
The Protector: You teaches the challenge's core scientific skill, telling a real pattern from chance, through a story-driven game built on the same NASA records as the website. Players open it by clicking the astronaut on the map.

1. The story. ORBI, a small satellite that "carries Earth's memory," asks the player to defeat THE STATIC, a force that whispers "it's just luck, don't worry," so that nobody acts.
2. The hero and the place. Players create their hero and choose a place on the world map.
3. Radar signals. The game shows the real changes measured there, for example "Rising Heat," with how much warmer the place has become since the record began.
4. Real pattern or just luck? For each signal, players examine the evidence. The game explains significance in plain words, for example "a pattern this strong would appear by luck less than 1 time in 1,000." It also reminds players that a trend shows what changed, not why.
5. Three rounds of decisions. Players answer in three rounds: Shield (protect yourself), Rally (protect your community) and Root (fix the root cause). Every wrong answer explains why it is weak.
6. Real Earth vs. Your Impact. Good choices weaken the problem in the player's world. A side-by-side view separates the unchanged NASA record ("Real Earth") from a clearly labelled what-if ("Your Impact") showing how the problem would ease if many people made the same choices.

Players can accept real-life pledges, earn ranks and stars, and play fully in English or Arabic.



Benefits :

  • Students and teachers: a ready-made lesson in reading data, testing trends and understanding the difference between correlation and causation.
  • Families and children: a game that builds climate awareness and practical protection habits, using real data from their own place, in English or Arabic.
  • The public and local planners: place-specific hazards with practical, area-appropriate protections and a clear timeline for action.

We want people to go beyond seeing environmental change to proving it, understanding it and acting on it. Every number comes from NASA data, and every result is explained in plain language.

WHAT SETS OUR SOLUTION APART:

- Scientific rigour. Our statistics were cross-checked against the established scientific libraries scipy, pymannkendall and pyhomogeneity, and the results agree.


- Honest about data quality. Wind speed was excluded on purpose: its only monthly NASA source shows an artificial jump around 2011 that a trend test would mistake for real change. A built-in break test flags similar problems in any series.
- Validated forecasts. Each projection is backtested against the last five years of observations before it is shown.
- Fully traceable. Every number can be checked by hand against the monthly CSV files included for every location.
- Works anywhere. The platform runs in any browser, on phones and offline, with no installation and no outside requests while it runs.
- One connected experience. The website and the game share the same NASA records, so learning and investigation reinforce each other.

Tools and Technologies Used

Coding Languages:

HTML, CSS, and JavaScript → Used to build the website and interactive game without requiring a build step. The platform can run offline using the data files stored within the project.

Python → Used to retrieve, process, and prepare NASA Earth science datasets.

Node.js → Used to calibrate and backtest environmental projections across different locations.

Libraries and Visualization Tools:

D3.js → Used to create the interactive globe, maps, and data visualizations.

Apache ECharts World Map Data → Used to display country outlines and geographical boundaries.

NumPy → Used for numerical data processing in Python.

Pillow and tifffile → Used to process satellite images and raster data.

Data Sources and Preparation:

NASA Giovanni API → Used to retrieve and explore NASA Earth science datasets.

NASA AppEEARS API → Used to access and process satellite-based environmental data.

Statistical Analysis and Trend Detection:

Seasonal Anomaly Detection → Environmental anomalies are calculated relative to the 2005–2020 mean to identify unusual changes.

Robust Z-Score (Median and MAD) → Used to detect unusually high or low monthly observations.

Pettitt Change-Point Test → Used to identify potential structural breaks in time-series data.

Mann–Kendall Test with Trend-Free Pre-Whitening → Used to detect statistically significant increasing or decreasing trends while accounting for serial correlation.

Sen’s Slope Estimator → Used to estimate the magnitude and rate of environmental change, with a 95% confidence interval.

Linear Regression and t-Test → Used as an additional approach to evaluate trends and their statistical significance.

Seasonal Mann–Kendall Test with Hirsch–Slack Correction → Used to assess trends while accounting for seasonal patterns.

Signal-to-Noise Ratio, Emergence Year, and Lag-1 Autocorrelation → Used to provide additional insight into the strength, timing, and persistence of environmental changes.

Environmental Projections and Validation:

Seasonal Sen’s Slope Projection → Used to estimate possible future trends with a 95% prediction range adjusted for autocorrelation.

Five-Year Backtesting → Each projection is evaluated against the last five years of historical observations before being displayed.

Node.js Calibration → Used to calibrate prediction ranges through backtesting across different geographical locations.

Earth Connections and Global Estimates:

Pearson Correlation → Used to investigate relationships between detrended and standardized annual environmental time series.

Area-Weighted Global Estimates → Used to calculate global averages from a 5° sample grid, accounting for differences in geographical area.
